title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in South
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust. The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC."We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday. Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said. It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder.  Chalk told Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that would include looking at whether any reports had been made but people or organisations had held back due to a "misplaced sense of cultural sensitivity".Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene. It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added. The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice.""We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement."Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review."There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.The review is due to report in five months. Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially".Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground.Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe.Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage.After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response.But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension".

schema.headline: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak

title: Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive
description: A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity.Ukrainian o
body: A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity.Ukrainian officials and Russia's defence ministry say the limited ceasefire is being respected. The truce, which the White House said was secured by US First Lady Melania Trump, is meant to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuation on Friday. Oleshky, along the front line in the Kherson region, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and on the other by Russian forces.Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.Many worry the truce will not hold, with one resident saying: "I don't believe in Russia's humanity."Oleshky, home to 24,000 people before the war, was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Ukraine now estimates some 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in the city and its surrounding areas.No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water for three years.Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies but has not had success in recent months, and it is deemed too dangerous to risk leaving on foot along mined roads out of the city. The ceasefire is supposed to allow supplies to reach the city and enable its roads to be cleared of mines to allow people safe passage out.One woman told the BBC she is in hospital recovering from two surgeries after stepping on a land mine."I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join Friday's planned evacuation.It is hard to make contact with people in Oleshky as communication is patchy and and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians, making it is difficult to verify reports the ceasefire is being implemented.Many details on the evacuations plans are unclear, initially including how and where to register for it. Some people want to know if they can bring their pets. Others are questioning what future they will have if they opt to leave their homes.While people are optimistic about leaving, there are also fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could see them be taken away and tortured. Someone who has been speaking to family in Oleshky said they fear shooting could restart during evacuations and Ukraine will somehow be blamed for not upholding the truce.Last month, the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.In response to the situation, the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire, with no details for how long it would last.Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, also confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun."As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.The White House said in the statement last week that "non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require".While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.In August 2025, she penned a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".While a truce is under way in Oleshky, elsewhere strikes continue. On Monday evening, attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv hit a university and a bridge, killing one person and injuring 14 others.In Russia, one person was killed and six others were injured after a Ukrainian drone strike on Bryansk.Additional reporting by Hafsa Khalil and Sareen Habeshian

schema.headline: Truce begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive

title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
description: Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, accor
body: Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event. Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month."Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin."These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."

schema.headline: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up

title: Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days
description: In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too cl
body: In recent years, many but not all politicians have approached the issue of Brexit like you or I might approach an electric fence. Avoid getting too close and, if needs must, climb over it gingerly.Burnham has no such reservations: he has repeatedly said in the last few weeks, let's talk about Brexit. He reckons the current deal between the UK and European Union isn't good enough.Over the weekend he went further, suggesting he wanted an "honest discussion" about freedom of movement. Countries in the EU's single market have to sign up to freedom of movement, which lets people live and work in all the countries that are part of it. Given how big a deal immigration was for many in the EU referendum in 2016, even reopening the question of freedom of movement feels like a big deal.On Monday morning, the prime minister appeared to add more detail, suggesting freedom of movement would only return in the UK having been sanctioned in a referendum. Later, though, his team wouldn't repeat that, instead emphasising that Burnham wants to start a broad based conversation – without at this point committing to any possible outcome.Some of his MPs felt this was a self-inflicted tangle he could have done without. Others see merit in Burnham's penchant for narrating his thoughts and possible direction publicly, thereby using his position to seek to dominate the political debate.While the Labour Party's centre of gravity tilts towards a collective instinct that a closer relationship with the EU would be preferable to the status quo, there are differences of emphasis and indeed outright disagreements about how much closer and when would be wise. Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen. This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East.The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects. But what about the Rosebank field, 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil?Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should.It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it. His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future."Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw. Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels? Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government – which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days

title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
description: Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.Her
body: Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example."She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William," wrote one commentator in 2020."Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it's too late," she was told on social media about her father.All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light.By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle, in a letter from her father's first wife, Roslyn Loveless.She says it is why she kept her distance and also why she didn't bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family. That letter was shared with Meghan by the police, at a time when she was classified as a working royal. It's not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her.And according to the Sussexes' spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was going ahead, presumably at a time when she was on official trips and having to put on a brave face.There was also criticism levelled at Meghan in December 2025 when her father was in hospital in the Philippines, undergoing the amputation of his leg. "I don't want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too," Markle told the Mail on Sunday at the time. There was a media storm about whether Meghan was going to reach out to her father, culminating in a letter being delivered from her to her father, which at the time was assumed to be well-wishes.But that whole episode now looks different with the benefit of hindsight. That letter was a much more fraught affair. It revealed that Meghan knew about the allegations against her father. We now understand that Meghan was telling him he would never see his grandchildren.Thomas Markle has strongly denied all the allegations against him, saying they are "sick lies" which are trying to destroy his reputation.His daughter Samantha Markle has also rejected the claims, saying the stories are "fake news" and "clickbait". "There will be no legal action against my dad with no evidence in so many flimsy stories and my dad never had access to any such content and was in the hospital most of the time that he was there," she wrote on X on Sunday.Samantha also challenges the credibility of the letter written by her mother, Roslyn Loveless, which was shared with Meghan in 2019 and contained details of allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle. When you look through photos of Meghan at events over the last seven years, you wonder what was going on behind the familiar smile.Those years have seen Netflix films, a tell-all memoir by Prince Harry, cookery series, podcasts and TV interviews. But a hidden narrative has been running in the background.Meghan's supporters have pointed to other factors in how she has been treated, with racism and sexism part of that toxic mix.But maybe there was also a sense of not knowing the authentic person behind the polished Brand Meghan.On Instagram, she has curated her life to look idyllic, but perhaps she'll get a more generous hearing now that her back story is as messy and imperfect as everyone else's.It could still be an uphill struggle to become more popular, beyond her own vocal, core group of supporters.A survey from YouGov earlier this month found 22% of people had a positive view of Meghan, compared with 49% who dislike her.That suggests there is still some way to go before Meghan fully wins the trust of the public. Fascination, yes. But affection, not always.For the British public, Californian Meghan hasn't always translated well.But perhaps this complex, still developing story - and the light it sheds on previous years - might mean there's a more rounded view of her in the future.

schema.headline: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?

title: Newspaper headlines: 'England's golden boy' and 'Time to pay fair'
description: Several of the papers lead on measures that are expected to be in the Budget.The Guardian says Chancellor John Healey will scrap what's seen as the cl
body: Several of the papers lead on measures that are expected to be in the Budget.The Guardian says Chancellor John Healey will scrap what's seen as the cliff-edge rule for unpaid carers, external. Currently they have to forfeit their entire week's carers' allowance - of more than £86 - if they earn just one penny above £204 in that week. The paper says that under the new rules, only £1 will be removed from the allowance for every £1 above the earning limit.On its front page the Times says Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4%, external for workers aged 21 and over, but not for those aged 18 to 21. The paper says that, in effect, spells the end for Labour's manifesto pledge to bring the minimum wage for younger people in line with that for older workers.The Daily Mirror highlights a call by trade unions for higher taxes on banks, external. The paper says bosses running Britain's big four banks take just two days to earn what a typical worker makes in a whole year. But the Daily Mail says raising taxes on banks would be "a folly in the extreme,", external because "for all their faults" the banks drive the economy, and if you tax them more heavily you punish every corporation and every small and medium-sized enterprise in the country.Charities providing end-of-life care have told the Daily Express that Healey should announce a £200m annual injection for their sector., external The paper says almost six-in-10 hospices in England have either made or are considering cuts to frontline services.According to the i Paper, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmoud is furious at Andy Burnham because members of the cabinet were not warned before he called for a debate, external about a return to freedom of movement with the EU. A government source told the paper the Prime Minister's comments had undermined Mahmood's strategy to reduce immigration. The Sun says restoring freedom of movement would be a catastrophe, external for getting the jobless back into work, for wages, public services and social cohesion.And the Daily Telegraph reports that guidance has been issued for teachers to help them uncover essays written by artificial intelligence., external The document lists dozens of words, phrases and stylistic features - such as "delve," "catalyst," and "in conclusion" - which, it says, could indicate use of AI tools, if they appear frequently.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'England's golden boy' and 'Time to pay fair'

title: My husband's death was hard enough - then came the admin
description: Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John meticulously planned the handover of household admin before his deathByJennifer MeierhansLouisa Nicoll
body: Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John meticulously planned the handover of household admin before his deathByJennifer MeierhansLouisa Nicoll knew her husband John was going to die about a year before it happened. The couple used the time to make memories with their children, James and Amy, and John meticulously organised their paperwork.But despite him asking for accounts to be switched to Louisa's name, she still received post addressed to him after his death. In one letter from their energy provider, it said: "Sorry you're leaving us. Is there anything we can do to make you stay?""I felt utterly exhausted, overwhelmed, frustrated and angry because of those experiences," she told BBC's Morning Live.Louisa now campaigns for changes in the way companies deal with admin after someone dies and offers advice on how talking about death before it happens can help families cope afterwards.Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, After their father's death, James and Amy still received texts from their mobile phone provider that read "Hi, John"  John was 50 and working as a police surveillance trainer when he was diagnosed with cancer. Louisa had a career in palliative care nursing and was a ward manager in a hospice. John underwent nine major surgeries and four rounds of chemotherapy - working full-time through it all."He absolutely loved working with his supportive police colleagues, and he cherished everyday family life and spending time with our friends," says Louisa.When further surgery was no longer an option, palliative chemotherapy was offered. Following many discussions, John decided to focus on making memories as a husband, dad and friend rather than spending his final months as a patient."He made a lovely speech at Amy's 18th birthday," she says. "We visited family in Scotland and had planned a family holiday to Greece - but Covid hit and we had a Greek night at home instead." The couple had a party for Louisa's 50th and their 25th wedding anniversary.Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John wrote Louisa an 18-page document called "things to make you smile"In the background, John was busy compiling a handover of the household admin."He even wrote a plan for me titled 'things you need to know', packed with every household account, insurance renewal and MOT dates," she says.He had emailed their energy provider saying he would like Louisa to take over as the account holder due to his terminal diagnosis.But instead, she was added as an additional name and had to close and reopen the account."I thought I was prepared for John's death but the reality was so much harder than I could ever have imagined. He really was the other half of me. So when I had to face the death admin, I felt so vulnerable without him beside me."James and Amy's mobile phone contracts were in John's name, too. They were asked to take his death certificate into a store but still received texts that read "Hi, John"."I'm sure nobody's doing this intentionally... but these companies could just get their bereavement services at a level that is not going to cause undue distress," says Louisa. "There should be a standardised practice."Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, Louisa urges families regardless of age to have conversations and make end-of-life plans Sarah Middlemiss, policy campaigns manager at end-of-life charity Marie Curie, tells Morning Live admin tasks can be particularly difficult when you are grieving."And because every company does things in a slightly different way and requires slightly different things, it can be really, really overwhelming," she says."Proper training on how to deal with people who are grieving or who are terminally ill in a really sensitive and timely manner would go a really long way."Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, John and Louisa at a family wedding before his diagnosisLouisa gives talks at events to encourage people to talk about death in advance."We plan for every major event in life - weddings, pregnancy, career changes, retirement, even our meals each day - yet most people leave the end of life completely to chance," she says."Our families end up trapped in a crisis - guessing our wishes in the back of an ambulance or a chaotic A&E department."She says she and John had those "hard but important conversations" long before they needed them.Image source, Louisa NicollImage caption, Louisa says John kept his sense of humour and personality throughout his treatmentJohn died peacefully at home in August 2020, just one day after their 26th wedding anniversary."Before he died, we spoke about what I would do for work after he died. He said, 'I think you'll tell our story, and show people that it is possible to live well when faced with dying.' And that is what I'm trying to do."How to get your affairs in orderGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: My husband's death was hard enough - then came the admin

title: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power
description: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.The Energy
body: A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 22,600 properties were still without power. Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.A yellow warning for strong winds came in effect on Monday evening across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland and expired on Tuesday morning. The Met Office has warned about the possibility of further power cuts and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England."Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," he told the BBC.He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

schema.headline: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power

title: Anti-social behaviour by neighbours has been 'hell', tenant says
description: For seven years James Daniel has been living next to successive "nightmare neighbours". Despite numerous complaints to various agencies, including his
body: For seven years James Daniel has been living next to successive "nightmare neighbours". Despite numerous complaints to various agencies, including his housing association, he said his situation had not improved. It comes as new data from the Housing Ombudsman showed a rise over five years in the number of complaints upheld about social landlords' handling of anti-social behaviour.While Devon and Cornwall Police has increased the number of closure orders placed on residential properties, housing associations report that dealing with anti-social behaviour can be a complex issue and requires working closely with other agencies. Daniel said he had spent years reporting the alleged anti-social behaviour and collecting evidence, including security camera and mobile phone footage, which he passed on to the police, North Devon Homes and now the BBC. The videos he shared with the BBC showed knives being thrown from a window, an altercation outside his house and a neighbour appearing to make gun gestures at his security camera.Other footage showed a previous tenant shouting at Daniel and other residents, as well as throwing bags of rubbish and a dust pan brush."Living next door to anti-social behaviour has been hell to be honest, absolute hell, said Daniel.New data showed the Housing Ombudsman upheld almost four times as many complaints relating to social landlords' handling of anti-social behaviour reports than five years ago.In the 2021-2022 financial year, the ombudsman found failings in 159 incidents compared with 609 in 2025–26.Ric Blakeway, the Housing Ombudsman at the time, said there were a number of "consistent reasons" why the maladministration rate - or uphold rate - had increased."It's poor communication, it's poor record keeping, it's not using the tools that landlords should use - such as doing a risk assessment or producing an action plan - and that is a consistent reason that we would uphold a case," he explained."Where we don't uphold it though, I think you see the kind of opposite of that."Easier access to the ombudsman service and greater awareness of housing rights were among the drivers Blakeway believed had led to a rise in casework.Blakeway said his teams had seen cases where residents had been making themselves "in effect homeless" by sleeping in cars to escape the anti-social behaviour.In West Cornwall, neighbours said closure orders on two properties in the same street had been effective. Melanie, whose surname we are not using, said residents had been "living in fear" before one neighbour, who was accused of waving a sword, was removed. "You shouldn't have to live like that these days," she said.At another property, PC James Tompson said officers spent weeks gathering evidence of drug use, fighting and anti-social behaviour linked to the address.In April, Daniel's neighbour was convicted of assaulting another resident and a month later was charged with allegedly harassing him.Daniel said victims of anti-social behaviour, particularly in social housing, needed support from agencies in a "more joined up approach"."For me, it's about highlighting the system is broken," he said."All the agencies are involved but actually it seems nobody's talking to each other, and nobody knows what's going on."He said he no longer felt safe at home and that it was becoming "impossible to get any support" for those affected by anti-social behaviour."It's got to the point where actually the house that I love, I don't love anymore," he added.

schema.headline: Anti-social behaviour by neighbours has been 'hell', tenant says

title: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy
description: Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.Polling published on Friday suggest
body: Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.But neither of their political blocs are projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a majority government - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.The campaign has been shaped by the issue of security - with the opposition bloc hammering Netanyahu for the unprecedented security failure that led to the 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken back to Gaza as hostages.They have pushed for an independent commission of inquiry into the attacks - something Netanyahu has long resisted, insisting it would be biased against him.Despite the opposition's attack lines, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security" - pointing to what he says are strategic victories in Israel's wars across the Middle East and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump. Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties who have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.Other leaders in the bloc include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a return to power will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history.There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.Eisenkot takes a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on Gaza, and has pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through a US-led peace plan or, if necessary, military means. Israel has continued to strike Gaza almost every day since a ceasefire was agreed last year, saying it is targeting Hamas operatives. The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 people since the start of the war, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel has faced growing international condemnation over its conduct in the war, and relations with its allies around the world have deteriorated.Eisenkot largely supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - which are illegal under international law - but wants to crack down on extremist Jewish settlers whose attacks are at an all-time high, according to UN figures. He has also spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or a state-minus" for Palestinians - under ultimate Israeli security control.The two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - has all but disappeared from mainstream Israeli politics. Though some have speculated the Arab parties may end up informally propping up an Eisenkot-led minority government - Lieberman, a key prospective member, has ruled out being part of such an arrangement.Red lines like these mean the electoral arithmetic is complex - but it remains to be seen what kind of concessions, deals and U-turns can be reached once the results come in. An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while hundreds of thousands are set to cast ballots for the first time.At 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly. Up and down the country, Israelis will gather to watch the results trickle in, with Netanyahu's Likud meeting in Jerusalem and Eisenkot's Yashar - formed only last year - assembling in Tel Aviv.Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists will also cast ballots, but many of those votes will not begin being counted until Wednesday - meaning there may be a late boon for the right-wing parties who are thought to have strong support from that demographic.Though often framed as a run-off between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, it is possible another leader could take power, if they were to withhold their party's support for a coalition unless given the top job.An outcome dreaded by many is political deadlock - where no bloc is able to reach a majority, and a minority government cannot be formed. In that scenario, new elections would be called, with Netanyahu to remain as interim prime minister. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

schema.headline: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy

title: Ballon d'Or Feminin: Alexia Putellas wins award for record-equalling third time
description: Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth con
body: Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year.Putellas, 32, captained Barcelona to Champions League glory as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July.She joins Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati on three Ballon d'Or Feminin crowns - her former Barcelona colleague won the award in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas did so in 2021 and 2022.The past six Ballons d'Or have been won by the Spanish pair, with Norway's Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spaniards to claim the prize.Putellas' latest victory caps a remarkable return to the pinnacle of world football after suffering a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in 2022."All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said."Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself."She collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across Fifa's top-50 ranked countries, with Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor coming second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third.Meanwhile, England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or, becoming the first English player to do so since Michael Owen in 2001.While Barcelona are always overwhelming favourites to win the three competitions on offer in Spain, Putellas' performances last season showed that she is still among the world's elite.Nicknamed 'La Reina' - meaning the queen - Putellas scored 21 goals and provided 13 assists in all competitions, ranking her third and second respectively among players across Europe's top five leagues.Seven of those goals came in the Women's Champions League as Barcelona claimed a fourth continental title in six seasons.Only Pernille Harder (eight), Alessia Russo (nine) and Ewa Pajor (11) scored more, all of whom are strikers by trade.But Putellas' contributions to Barcelona's attacking play went far beyond scoring goals herself.In Liga F - which Barcelona won for a seventh consecutive season - she finished joint-sixth for assists (seven) and fourth for open-play chances created (40).Across Europe's top five leagues, only Claudia Pina (199), Vicky Lopez (183) and Georgia Stanway (168) recorded more sequence involvements ending in an open-play shot than Putellas (151).In all competitions, she created more chances (89, 19 of which were big chances) and completed more passes ending in the final third (965) than any other player in Liga F, the Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de Espana.Only Bayern Munich's Klara Buhl created as many chances as Putellas in the Champions League last season (36), the most by a player in a single edition of the competition since Caroline Graham Hansen in 2021-22 (38).Putellas was born and grew up in the Catalan municipality of Mollet del Valles, about 12 miles north-east of Barcelona.She began playing football in the street, and soon became a Barcelona fan and a regular attendee at Camp Nou.With matches always on the TV at home, former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta and Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho quickly became her idols.After attending a summer football camp run by Xavi and playing for local side CE Sabadell, Putellas spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy.Spells at Espanyol and Levante followed the disbandment of her girls team, before she eventually returned to Barca in 2012.Cue the start of a 14-year career with her childhood club during which she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European cups.But after winning the Ballon d'Or for the first time in 2021, one of the toughest moments of Putellas' career came when she suffered an ACL injury on the eve of Euro 2022, ruling her out of the tournament.Though she retained the Ballon d'Or later that year, it took a while for her to return to her best level. Playing only a bit-part role in Spain's triumphant 2023 World Cup campaign would have stung.After scoring in the 2024 Champions League final and improving further the following season, in 2025-26 she shouldered much of Barcelona's creative burden as Aitana Bonmati missed five months through injury and ended the season a quadruple winner.If that was not enough, the midfielder scored twice in a 4-0 thrashing of England in June that secured Spain's place at the 2027 World Cup at the Lionesses' expense.With her contract at Barcelona expiring and keen for a fresh challenge, Putellas made the decision to leave her childhood club. She, and her fans, were distraught.She had several offers from England, Mexico and the United States, but joined the ambitious project of US billionaire Michelle Kang at London City Lionesses in July."I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player," Putellas told BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast in August.With three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new club, it is clear Putellas is still deserving of her nickname.

schema.headline: Ballon d'Or Feminin: Alexia Putellas wins award for record-equalling third time

title: Harry Kane: Bayern Munich and England striker wins Ballon d'Or after record season
description: Harry Kane has become the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001 after being crowned the world's best player at a cere
body: Harry Kane has become the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001 after being crowned the world's best player at a ceremony in London.The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker is the fifth Englishman to win in total, with Stanley Matthews (1956), Bobby Charlton (1966) and Kevin Keegan (1978 and 1979) the others.Denis Law of Scotland (1964) and Northern Ireland's George Best (1968) are the other winners from the United Kingdom.Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second, while Barcelona and Spain attacker Lamine Yamal completed the top three."Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane told Dazn."I had to go through many ups and downs, especially early in my career. I was never the person that people thought was going to be the superstar like some of the guys now."I had to bide my time and work hard, a lot of times it was me against my own mind and I had to come through it, I had to show self-belief, determination. "I think that grounded me even when I did make it at the highest level to keep improving and keep getting better."England manager Thomas Tuchel said he was "delighted" to see Kane win the award as he hailed the forward's success as a "huge honour".Prince William, meanwhile, said the former Tottenham Hotspur player was a "brilliant captain" and "remarkable player".Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches last season, the most a Bayern player has ever struck in one campaign. Including England matches, it was 73 goals - plus eight assists - in 65 matches.Only one player at a club in Europe's top five leagues has ever scored more goals in a season.But he wins it despite not lifting either of football's biggest prizes last season, having lost in both the World Cup and Champions League semi-finals.Remarkably the Three Lions captain becomes the first Bayern player to win the Ballon d'Or since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981.To celebrate Kane's success, the Wembley arches were lit up in gold on Monday night.BBC Sport looks at why Kane won it and how unusual it is to do so without securing one of those major trophies.In terms of trophies, Kane may have 'only' lifted the German double last season. But that more than doubled his career trophy total - having also won the Bundesliga the season before.But in terms of individual output Kane - whose previous best Ballon d'Or finish was 10th - was unmatched last season.His 61 goals in all competitions for Bayern was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five leagues managed.In fact it was the most anyone has recorded since Cristiano Ronaldo also notched 61 for Real Madrid 11 years ago.He was the Bundesliga's top scorer with 36 goals - 17 clear of anyone else. In the Champions League he scored 14 for the beaten semi-finalists.In the German Cup he scored 10 goals, including a hat-trick in the 3-0 win over Stuttgart in the final, and he also netted once in the German Super Cup.No player has ever scored so many goals in a season for Bayern, a club who have had legendary goalscorers like Gerd Muller, Rummenigge and more recently Robert Lewandowski in their ranks.Kane's 12 goals for England last season - including six at the World Cup - take him up to a total of 73.Only one player in history from Europe's top leagues has scored more in a season, Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.Next on the list are Muller (72 in 1972-73), Cristiano Ronaldo (66 in both 2011-12 and 2014-15), former Brazil striker Ronaldo (66 in 1996-97), Erling Haaland (64 in 2022-23) and Luis Suarez (64 in 2015-16).Former England striker Alan Shearer recently told BBC Sport: "The winner of the Ballon d'Or should be Harry Kane. "His numbers for the last 12 to 18 months have been absolutely sensational for Bayern and for England. For that reason, he should get it."Another ex-Three Lions player Danny Murphy added: "His goalscoring has been relentless, brilliant. He's had one of the best seasons of his career and it'll be a great reward for him if he gets the trophy."He's been brilliant at Bayern Munich since he's been there, adapted really well and he's been the best centre forward in the world for the last 12 months."The Ballon d'Or was only available to European players from its formation in 1956 until 1995 when it was opened up to everyone.Since then in four of the seven World Cup years, the Ballon d'Or has been awarded to a world champion - including Messi in 2023 (as the 2022 World Cup was in the winter).However, that was the first time since 2006 it had happened, with Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo and Luka Modric all winning since then despite not winning the World Cup that year.This is only the fifth time in the past 20 years that the Ballon d'Or has not gone to a player who has won either the World Cup, the Champions League or a European Championship/Copa America - with Kane joining Messi (three times) and Ronaldo.Lamine Yamal, who won the World Cup with Spain, had been one of the favourites but lost out to Kane.Last year, winning the Champions League helped PSG and France's Ousmane Dembele to the crown.Kane may have just won the Ballon d'Or but some are already wondering if he is in a good place to retain it next year.The striker has scored 10 goals in his opening 12 games for Bayern this season. Throw in six goals in four Nations League games for England and that is a total of 16 in 16 matches so far.Bayern are unbeaten in the Bundesliga and Champions League this season.If they were to win a Treble - and Kane keeps scoring at about a goal a game - it would be tough to look past him, especially in a season with no World Cup, European Championship or Copa America.The last player other than Messi or Ronaldo to win it two years in a row was Marco van Basten in 1988 and 1989.However, Lamine Yamal will be hoping to make it to the top, having now finished second and third over the past two years.He has started the season in electric form, with 10 goals and 10 assists in 13 games  for Barcelona in La Liga and the Champions League. And Barca are currently favourites to win the Champions League, which could ultimately end up being a deciding factor.He would be the youngest player to win the Ballon d'Or - aged 20 - if he does lift it next year.Real Madrid's Mbappe will also fancy his chances of winning for the first time, with 14 goals in 13 appearances for club and country.The youngest winner remains Brazilian Ronaldo, who was 21 when he won in 1997. Arsenal, who have never had a Ballon d'Or winner, and Paris St-Germain are two of the other frontrunners to win the Champions League.

schema.headline: Harry Kane: Bayern Munich and England striker wins Ballon d'Or after record season

title: What do you want from the Budget? 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40'
description: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma Crew
body: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma CrewUpdated 2 hours agoChancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice.Chloe's biggest worry is the cost of living. Her husband passed away four years ago and she's bringing up their 16-year-old son alone.She's very grateful the rent for her south London maisonette is subsidised through a housing association, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."Her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity."We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families."I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."'I earn £22,000. Saving for a house is impossible'Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.   "Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax. He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently. He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."'I get £338 UC per month. I'm trying my best'Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college. The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers."I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee, external scheme extended.The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."'I earn £30,000 and dread filling up my car'Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump."The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."'I earn £150,000 and would be happy to pay more tax'Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year."I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors."If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."'I have a £15,000 pension. I'm spending more of my savings'Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her. "It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look at removing standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit, external, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: What do you want from the Budget? 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40'

title: F1 Q&A: Antonelli dominance, Hamilton eyes Africa GP & Albon form
description: This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achiev
body: This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achieve the same success. There is a theme throughout the season. How much of that is down to driver ability, driving style etc and how much is down to car set-up and strategy. Is George better than this or has he reached his limit? - JulianThe dominant theme of the 2026 season has been the degree to which Kimi Antonelli has stepped up his game after a mixed rookie season that contained some definite highs, but also quite a few difficulties.In doing so, he has overwhelmed George Russell, who has accepted and is more than willing to say that Antonelli has simply done a better job than him this season.Antonelli's performances this year have lived up to the billing with which he came to F1 - that he could be the sport's next generational talent.He has had some luck, and some of his wins have turned on fortune - safety cars in Japan and Madrid, for example.But he has also performed at a level of consistent excellence, and produced some absolutely standout performances, most obviously Monaco, Monza and Austin.The Mercedes has on average been the best car, but Antonelli is the only one of the team's two drivers who has always been a factor. He fully deserves the world title that he is almost certain to clinch this weekend in Mexico City.As for Russell, he has fundamentally used driving style as an explanation for his relative struggles, saying the previous cars suited his, and the new ones Antonelli's. He has won only three races compared with Antonelli's nine.On Sunday, team principal Toto Wolff said Russell had struggled in Austin to get the right set-up on the Mercedes with the new upgrade package, which has been problematic since it was introduced in Malaysia.Wolff said: "George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category and merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year."This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles and he struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us."We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case."So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all about the intelligence, the ability, the determination."Driving style and set-up are genuine reasons for a driver to struggle in certain circumstances.However, it's also a case that the absolute elite, the all-time greats - drivers such as Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso - tend to find a way to be at the top of their game regardless of the car's behaviour.The worry for Russell right now is that if Antonelli is at that level - and it looks as though he has the potential to be, given his performances in only his second season - he will have his work cut out to beat him consistently in the future.So he needs to regroup over the winter, come back next year and prove he can get back on to Antonelli's level.With Lewis Hamilton's intentions clear of staying in F1 until there is an African Grand Prix, which I think will most likely be with Ferrari, what does that mean for the young talents who desire to drive for Ferrari? Will it be at least another four to five years before we see new drivers replacing either or both Lewis and Charles Leclerc? - LiamLewis Hamilton repeated in Austin last weekend that, ideally, he would like to still be racing when Formula 1 returns to Africa."I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," he said."So, yes, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."Whether he can manage to stay that long is another question.Formula 1 has said the African Grand Prix in Rwanda will be held in the "early 2030s".The aim is for that to be in 2030 but it's not clear whether the new track will be ready by then.Even if they make that deadline, will Hamilton still be racing? He will be 45 at the start of 2030. That's the same age as Fernando Alonso is now, and he is still going strong.Hamilton's answer alludes to his current contract, which it is believed lasts until the end of 2027. So he would need to do another one of three years to make it to 2030.As he says, if he is still performing at the level he is now by the middle of next year, why not? But as yet it's not clear what Ferrari will think about that.Hamilton's presence - and the long-term contract held by team-mate Charles Leclerc - does raise questions about Ferrari's driver academy.First and foremost, those questions surround Oliver Bearman, who is yet to finalise his new contract with Haas for next season.Bearman has had a strong season and a new deal is believed to be pretty much a formality - driver and team have expressed their desire to stay together, and the Briton was talking in a BBC 5 live interview at the weekend very much as if he would still be a Haas driver next year. But Bearman has higher ambitions than staying at Haas for the rest of his career.If Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be at Ferrari for the next four years, Bearman would have every right to be asking the team what that means for him.If he isn't going to get into the senior team, what can they do to further his career? Do they let him go, so he can pursue his ambitions elsewhere, or do they allow him to do that while still maintaining links?These questions become even more pressing for Bearman now Brazilian Rafael Camara - also a Ferrari young driver - is joining Haas for 2027.Bearman needs to beat the Brazilian if he is not to face an existential threat to his future as a potential driver for a top team.What's been happening with Alex Albon this season? Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz seems to have the better of him, and the car doesn't look to be in a good place. - DavidOf the two Williams drivers, in a team that is struggling, Carlos Sainz has had the better season.But it's not as stark as it perhaps appears just looking on the surface.Sainz leads Albon by two points in the championship, and while the qualifying comparison is skewed heavily towards Sainz on a head-to-head basis at 13-5, the time gap between them is 0.115 seconds.As if Albon was not already having a rough season, to top it he incurred the wrath of Fernando Alonso in Austin after the two collided on the first lap, leaving both with damaged cars.Alonso said: "The quality of the drivers in the lower third of the grid is very low, as we saw today with Alex."Williams are in such a state this year that comparing the drivers should be treated with a degree of qualification.The car has been slow, and the team have struggled with consistency between parts, as well as quality and degradation.In other words, two parts that should perform the same have not always done so, and some of them wear out and lose performance quicker than others.Of course that works across both drivers but it does make comparisons difficult.Albon was asked about the comparison with Sainz in qualifying in Monza last month.He pointed out that the crash he had in Canada when he hit a groundhog had been costly because there was a new engine in the car that weekend, which was written off. That meant he had to run an old engine longer than ideal.And he alluded to Williams suffering from the same issues with varying engine performance that happened in the early days of the new engine rules at Mercedes and McLaren."There's a few things," Albon said. "In the beginning of the year, it was very battery-dominated."If you think even just the George and Kimi situation, that's the manufacturer side of it having issues. So you can imagine it's not just them two that have had problems."There's been a few qualifying sessions where the corners have been good, but you don't see it in the lap time. It's on the stopwatch."And then we're also going through our own issues as a team. And that's not just on my side. There's also a side where to say that both cars are performing in the same way would not be true. We've been fighting some inconsistencies in the cars that's been there since the beginning of the year."We're much better now at getting on top of them. If you look at the last four or five weekends, we're actually very close in terms of performance. But it's taken a while to get there."Do you foresee a world in which live F1 coverage ever returns to free-to-air telly in the UK or is it now stuck behind a paywall for eternity? I've now taken a different career path but becoming an engineer in F1 was my ultimate ambition when I was applying for university in the early 2010s, inspired by BBC's live coverage. - IanIn the UK, the current situation is that Sky has exclusive rights to broadcast F1 behind a paywall, while Channel 4 has highlights on free-to-air television, with live coverage of the British Grand Prix.Sky has the rights until the end of 2034, after it struck a new deal for a larger fee earlier this year.That came in the wake of Apple buying the US rights starting from this season.At the same time, the television market is in flux as streaming becomes increasingly prevalent as a means of consuming content.In that context, as well as the wider sports broadcast situation, it's hard to imagine a situation where F1 could return fully to free-to-air television.The wider picture is it is still on free-to-air in some countries - Brazil as an example.But F1 would also argue free-to-air does not always mean more people getting sight of the sport, depending on how it's promoted in various ways, and viewing habits are not the same in all countries.Social media output is also an important consideration. At the same time, F1 is a business that exists to make money.
